  "ideas": [
    {
      "name": "Multi-Jury Projection Review",
      "levels": ["community"],
      "mechanism": "Generate multiple candidate projections for a single video clip using different random seeds. Instead of a single VLM critic, use three Jev instances to score each candidate on three distinct typed rubrics (e.g., 'object_fidelity', 'spatial_coherence', 'motion_correctness'). The winning projection is the one with the highest *total score* across the Jev juries. This is a community of critics agreeing on the best local perspective.",
      "jev_role": "Jev will be used as a jury of three experts. For each projection, three Jev requests will be made: one asking `score(projection_text, rubric='object_fidelity')`, one `score(..., rubric='spatial_coherence')`, and one `score(..., rubric='motion_correctness')`. The scores are summed to create a total fidelity score for that projection.",
      "hypothesis": "The total fidelity of the projection selected by the multi-Jev jury will be higher than the fidelity of the projection selected by a single VLM critic. This would be confirmed if the jury-selected projection's fidelity is > 0.45, refuted if it is < 0.35.",
      "cost": "For 10 video clips, 3 (projections) * 3 (Jev questions) * 10 (clips) = 90 Jev calls. The final evaluation of the best projection with the VLM is 10 calls. Total ~100 calls, dominated by Jev.",
      "beyond_classic_ml": "This replaces a single, expensive global evaluation (VLM) with a consensus of many cheap, typed, local evaluations, distributing the judgment across a community of agents."
    },
    {
      "name": "Edge Glyph Emergence",
      "levels": ["tissue", "organ"],
      "mechanism": "Instead of hand-defining the set of edge glyphs, start with a minimal set and let a Jev 'organ' propose new glyphs. The process is: 1) A 'tissue' level projects the scene with the current glyph set. 2) The organ sends this text to Jev, asking `choice(representation_problem='poor_edge_detail', options=['keep', 'propose_new_glyph'])`. 3) If 'propose_new_glyph', Jev generates a description of a missing edge feature, which is converted to a new byte-exact glyph for the tissue to use in the next iteration.",
      "jev_role": "Jev acts as a developmental organ. For each projected frame, it is asked to make a choice: `choice(representation_problem='poor_edge_detail', options=['keep', 'propose_new_glyph'])`. If it chooses to propose, it also answers `noul(question='is_this_a_useful_edge_feature?', context=new_glyph_description)` to validate its own creation.",
      "hypothesis": "Iteratively allowing Jev to propose new glyphs will increase the fidelity score of the projection over a fixed number of iterations. This is confirmed if the fidelity after 5 proposal cycles exceeds 0.40, refuted if it remains below 0.32.",
      "cost": "For 5 iterations on 10 clips: 5 * 10 = 50 Jev calls for the choice, plus up to 50 for the noul check if all proposals are accepted. Total ~100 Jev calls. The projector recompilation is free as it's deterministic C.",
      "beyond_classic_ml": "This allows structure (the set of glyphs) to grow organically through guided development, where a cheap typed agent creates new features to solve local representation problems, rather than being fixed by a designer."
    },
    {
      "name": "Motion Arrow Auction",
      "levels": ["family"],
      "mechanism": "For each frame sequence, generate a dense field of possible motion vectors. Then, have a 'family' of three Jev agents compete to 'claim' these vectors. Each Jev agent is given a different, overlapping subset of the frame. They each ask `choice(motion_vector_claim='vector_XY', options=['claim', 'ignore'], rubric='motion_confidence_in_my_region')`. The winning vector is the one claimed by the Jev agent with the highest confidence score. The family collectively builds the final motion arrow field.",
      "jev_role": "Three Jev agents form a family. For a set of candidate motion vectors, each agent is asked to evaluate a different subset. For each vector, they answer `choice(motion_vector_claim='vector_XY', options=['claim', 'ignore'])` and simultaneously `score(rubric='motion_confidence_in_my_region')` for that vector. The vector is assigned to the agent with the highest confidence score.",
      "hypothesis": "A motion field constructed by this competitive family of Jev agents will achieve a higher motion recall score than one created by a simple heuristic or a single Jev agent evaluating all vectors. This is confirmed if the motion recall exceeds 0.35, refuted if it is below 0.25.",
      "cost": "For 10 clips, 3 (agents) * 20 (candidate vectors/clip) * 2 (choice and score) = 120 Jev calls. The final VLM evaluation is 10 calls. Total ~130 calls.",
      "beyond_classic_ml": "This replaces a central decision (one agent for all motion) with a decentralized negotiation (a family of agents for local motion), where structure emerges from localized competition rather than a global plan."
    },
    {
      "name": "Quantum-Guided Projection Search",
      "levels": ["cell"],
      "mechanism": "The search over projector parameters (e.g., brightness thresholds, glyph placements) is a high-dimensional space. Use MothQuantum to generate a small set of random parameter seeds. Each seed represents a 'cell' with a unique first-person view of how to project. Have each 'cell' project a single held-out clip and use Jev to ask `score(projection_text, rubric='holistic_fidelity')`. The 'cell' with the highest score 'survives' and its parameters become the new baseline for the next generation of quantum-random mutations.",
      "jev_role": "Each 'cell' (a parameter set) creates a projection and sends it to Jev. The Jev acts as the cell's internal sense of quality, answering `score(projection_text, rubric='holistic_fidelity')` to evaluate its own 'viewpoint'. The score determines if the cell's perspective is valid.",
      "hypothesis": "A genetic search guided by Jev's evaluation of quantum-randomly generated projector parameters will find a configuration with higher fidelity than brute-force search over a larger, non-random set. This is confirmed if the best fidelity found in 50 generations is > 0.50, refuted if it is < 0.38.",
      "cost": "For 50 generations, 10 (cells/gen) * 1 (score/cell) = 500 Jev calls. Quantum random bytes are free in simulator. The final evaluation is 1 call. Total ~500 calls, dominated by Jev.",
      "beyond_classic_ml": "This mimics cellular evolution, where cheap, randomized local viewpoints (cells) are selected for their viability based on a simple typed judgment, allowing structure (projector config) to grow through mutation and selection without a loss function gradient."
    }
  ]
}

request.content:
We have a working research harness that turns a camera feed (short frame sequences) into plain text ("projections": character art with edge glyphs, braille, motion arrows). A vision-language model reconstructs the scene (objects, positions, motion) from the text alone; agreement with ground truth is the projection's fidelity. We measured: brightness-only text 0.18, edge glyphs following edges 0.34, motion arrows over edges 0.33 with motion recall 0.27, a VLM reading the real frames 0.92. Search over projector configs is noise-limited; averaging three VLM critics and promoting on held-out feeds fixed overfitting.

Tools available right now, all via API:
- TypeSafe "Jev": a SYSTEM-ONE model that answers TYPED questions about any state (text or JSON) in ~150 ms: noul (probability yes/no), choice (pick one named option, with probabilities), score (expected value on a rubric of levels). Many named questions can be asked in ONE request about the same state. Very cheap. It cannot see images.
- DeepInfra: vision-language models (Qwen3-VL, Gemma-3, Mistral-Small), large LLMs (Kimi-K2.6, Qwen3-235B, gpt-oss-120b, MiniMax-M3, DeepSeek), CLIP / text embeddings.
- MothQuantum: certified quantum random bytes (slow on real hardware, fast in simulator).
- Everything deterministic in the projector kernel is byte-exact integer C, so any device reproduces it.

The research vision: go beyond classic RL / neural nets / backprop. Learning as a HOLARCHY of first-person perspectives — cells -> tissues -> organs -> organisms -> families -> communities — with no central authority: a murmuration or kaleidoscope of many cheap viewpoints that see reality from different angles, help each other locally, and grow structure (guided growth) rather than being trained end-to-end. Typed system-one judgments are the "nerve impulses"; expensive models are rare "deliberations".

Propose 4 CONCRETE, NOVEL experiments that can be run THIS WEEK with exactly these tools on this projection problem (we have ground truth, so results are measurable). Each must use Jev in an essential, non-trivial way, name the level(s) of organization it lives at, and state a falsifiable hypothesis with the number that would confirm or refute it. Prefer ideas where many cheap local typed judgments replace one expensive global one, where structure grows, or where perspectives negotiate without a center.

Reply with JSON only:
{"ideas": [{"name": "<short>", "levels": ["cell"|"tissue"|"organ"|"organism"|"family"|"community"], "mechanism": "<3-5 sentences>", "jev_role": "<what Jev is asked, typed>", "hypothesis": "<falsifiable, with the measurement>", "cost": "<API calls estimate>", "beyond_classic_ml": "<one sentence: why this is not just RL/NN/backprop>"}]}
